title: Multilingual Brain Decoding Reveals Shared Cortical Semantic Geometry
summary: Human languages differ markedly in lexical and syntactic form yet can convey similar semantic content. The neural basis of this cross-language semantic commonality remains unclear. Here we developed a multilingual brain decoding framework and analysed brain recordings from 227 participants spanning Chinese, English and French. We found that cortical semantic representations exhibited consistent semantic geometry relationships across languages and individuals, revealing a shared cortical semantic geometry. Importantly, the cross-language consistency of cortical semantic geometry increased from sensorimotor to higher-order association cortex, forming a shared semantic geometry gradient closely aligned with the principal cortical functional gradient. Our work establishes generalizable multilingual brain decoding and identifies stable cortical semantic geometry as a neural basis for semantic commonality across languages.

AI.tldr: Brain recordings from 227 Chinese, English and French speakers reveal a shared cortical semantic geometry that grows more consistent across languages from sensorimotor toward higher-order association cortex, mirroring the brain's principal functional gradient.
AI.motivation: Languages differ greatly in lexical and syntactic form yet convey similar semantic content, but the neural basis of this cross-language semantic commonality is unclear.
AI.method: Developed a multilingual brain decoding framework and analysed brain recordings from 227 participants across Chinese, English and French.
AI.result: Cortical semantic representations showed consistent semantic geometry across languages and individuals, forming a shared cortical semantic geometry. Cross-language consistency increased from sensorimotor to higher-order association cortex, yielding a shared semantic geometry gradient aligned with the principal cortical functional gradient.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes generalizable multilingual brain decoding and identifies stable cortical semantic geometry as a neural basis for semantic commonality across languages.

title: Cross-disorder Learning of Imaging-derived Joint Mophometric Markers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases
summary: As two most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) shared commonalities both in symptomology and pathophysiology. However, to what extent and in what way these two distinct disorders overlap remain underexplored. In this study, we propose an explicit, interpretable and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to elucidate the morphometric biomarkers linked to AD and PD. We applied such high-dimensional machine learning model to two most popular open-source neuroimaging datasets, i.e., Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). On the one hand, our cross-disorder classifier revealed neuro-anatomical alteration patterns well aligning with previous neuroimaging research findings and underscoring patients' clinical presentations. On the other hand, the spatially adaptive trained classifier using shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to respective individual models, which further highlights the cross-disorder framework's efficacy on modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an interpretable, spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to identify morphometric biomarkers common to and distinct between Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), leveraging the shared structure between the two neurodegenerative disorders.
AI.motivation: AD and PD share similarities in symptomology and pathophysiology, yet the extent and manner of their overlap remain underexplored. Existing work lacks an explicit, interpretable approach to model cross-disorder relationships, especially under limited-size datasets.
AI.method: An explicit, interpretable, and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework using high-dimensional machine learning, applied to two open-source neuroimaging datasets (ADNI for AD and PPMI for PD). A shared prior enables transfer across disease domains, and a cross-disorder classifier is trained to extract morphometric biomarkers.
AI.result: The cross-disorder classifier revealed neuroanatomical alteration patterns aligning well with prior neuroimaging findings and patients' clinical presentations. The spatially adaptive classifier trained with the shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to the respective individual models.
AI.conclusion: The cross-disorder transfer learning framework is effective for modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains and offers an interpretable way to characterize shared and disease-specific morphometric biomarkers of AD and PD.

title: Caterpillar trees are asymmetric, balanced trees are symmetric
summary: Two conjectures of Allman, Long and Rhodes are proven. The ultrametric exchangeable model captures the symmetries in allele distributions of ultrametric mechanistic models of coalescence and substitution in mathematical phylogeny. The dimension of this model with respect to the species tree leaf count is shown to be greatest for caterpillar trees and least for balanced trees.

AI.tldr: The paper proves two conjectures of Allman, Long and Rhodes concerning the dimension of the ultrametric exchangeable model in mathematical phylogeny, showing the model dimension is largest for caterpillar species trees and smallest for balanced species trees.
AI.motivation: Ultrametric exchangeable models capture the symmetries in allele distributions arising from ultrametric mechanistic models of coalescence and substitution in phylogenetics. Two conjectures by Allman, Long and Rhodes about how the model's dimension depends on tree shape were previously unresolved; this work aims to settle them.
AI.method: The authors establish proofs of the two conjectures, analyzing the dimension of the ultrametric exchangeable model as a function of the number of species tree leaves, comparing caterpillar (highly unbalanced) and balanced tree topologies.
AI.result: The model dimension is shown to be greatest for caterpillar trees and least for balanced trees, confirming both conjectures.
AI.conclusion: The dimension of the ultrametric exchangeable model depends strongly on species tree shape, attaining extremal values at caterpillar and balanced trees; the Allman–Long–Rhodes conjectures hold.

title: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle
summary: Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket---a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior---can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, and reproduce. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well, with qualifications. A flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior. Flux removes only part of the linear dependence, and a nonlinear test shows that conditioning on flux \emph{increases} the dependence, consistent with conditioning on a collider, since flux is a joint function of concentrations on both sides of the boundary. The dependence is concentrated within about one organism radius of the boundary. A band of the surrounding field that thick screens the interior from the exterior beyond it, as any short-range field would, which is not evidence of inference.

AI.tldr: The authors test whether a flux-defined Markov blanket in a self-replicating reaction-diffusion system actually screens interior from exterior (the free energy principle's key condition). It largely fails: flux conditioning increases dependence (collider effect), and the observed "screening" band is just short-range field behavior, not evidence of inference.
AI.motivation: Friston's free energy principle claims systems bounded by a Markov blanket perform approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. This claim has rarely been tested in concrete nonlinear systems, so the authors ask whether a physically defined blanket in a pattern-forming system really satisfies the screening condition.
AI.method: They study self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model (persisting, competing, reproducing) and test the blanket condition by checking directed boundary exchange and timescale separation, then evaluating a flux-defined blanket via linear dependence removal and a nonlinear conditioning test.
AI.result: Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well with qualifications. The flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior: flux removes only part of linear dependence, and conditioning on flux increases dependence, consistent with a collider effect since flux is a joint function of both sides. Dependence concentrates within ~one organism radius of the boundary. A thick surrounding band screens as any short-range field would, which is not evidence of inference.
AI.conclusion: The blanket condition is not satisfied by a flux-defined boundary in this system, and apparent screening by a surrounding band is merely a generic short-range effect rather than evidence of approximate Bayesian inference, qualifying the free energy principle's blanket claims.

title: Reading Between the Reads: A Decade On, Revisiting Sequencing Protocol Annotation in the Sequence Read Archive
summary:
Background: Experimental metadata are essential for interpreting archived sequencing data. In 2015, Alnasir and Shanahan examined the annotation of fragmentation, adapter ligation and enrichment in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA). This study revisits those measurements using the original SQL keyword definitions on a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema.
  Results: The contemporary database contained 41,593,302 experiments, compared with 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three historical keyword groups declined from 4.06% to 1.42%. The protocol field was NULL in 67.65% of contemporary experiments. Searching design_description alongside the protocol field increased combined three-step keyword detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most additional matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage varied across sequencing library strategies, ranging from 0.26% for AMPLICON to 7.69% for RNA-Seq. Independent comparison of 150 sampled experiment records against source XML confirmed agreement in all historical keyword classifications.
  Conclusions: The original criteria identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade earlier. Additional preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limitations of searches restricted to one metadata field. Differences among sequencing strategies complicate historical comparisons as preparation methods evolve. The findings support more consistent protocol annotation and the need to distinguish keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.

AI.tldr: A 2026 re-analysis of NCBI SRA metadata using the original 2015 SQL keyword criteria finds that the share of experiments documenting all three preparation steps (fragmentation, adapter ligation, enrichment) in the library_construction_protocol field fell from 4.06% to 1.42%, partly because that field is NULL in 67.65% of records; adding design_description raises detection to 2.88%, and coverage varies widely by library strategy (0.26% AMPLICON to 7.69% RNA-Seq).
AI.motivation: Experimental metadata are needed to interpret archived sequencing data, but annotation practice may have changed since Alnasir and Shanahan's 2015 audit of SRA fragmentation, adapter ligation, and enrichment annotations. This study asks whether the original measurements still hold a decade later, using identical keyword definitions to enable direct comparison.
AI.method: The original 2015 SQL keyword definitions were reapplied to a September 2026 NCBI metadata snapshot reconstructed in the historical SRAdb schema. The library_construction_protocol field was searched for the three historical keyword groups, then supplemented with the design_description field. Results were stratified by sequencing library strategy, and 150 sampled experiment records were independently checked against source XML.
AI.result: The database held 41,593,302 experiments versus 419,620 in 2013. In library_construction_protocol, the proportion matching all three keyword groups dropped from 4.06% to 1.42%, and the field was NULL in 67.65% of experiments. Combining design_description with the protocol field raised three-step detection to 1,197,367 experiments (2.88%), with most extra matches occurring where the protocol field was NULL. Coverage ranged from 0.26% (AMPLICON) to 7.69% (RNA-Seq). The 150-record XML validation showed full agreement with all historical keyword classifications.
AI.conclusion: The original criteria now identify a smaller proportion of experiments in the designated protocol field than a decade ago. Preparation-related terminology is detectable in general experiment descriptions, exposing the limits of single-field searches. Variation across sequencing strategies complicates historical comparison as preparation methods evolve. The authors call for more consistent protocol annotation and for distinguishing keyword occurrence from the adequacy of experimental documentation.

title: EMBER: Predicting TCR--pMHC Binding Without a Docked Complex
summary: We propose EMBER, a structure-based framework for TCR--pMHC binding prediction that eliminates the need for a predicted docked complex, and with it the placement error that dominates such predictions. Traditional structure-based predictors utilize the co-folded complex structure of the receptor and the antigen and interpret binding from its contact surface. Consequently, every downstream feature inherits any deviation the structure-prediction tool introduced. Methodologically, EMBER folds the TCR and pMHC independently, encodes them as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, and compares their learned representations without constructing a shared coordinate frame. A relative pose is therefore not an input of the model, so placement error cannot propagate into the prediction. Computationally, EMBER preprocesses $O(N{+}M)$ monomer folds where a complex-based predictor needs $O(NM)$ operations. Experimentally, under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER is first on every metric under all four folding tools, by 0.9 to 14.4% in micro-AUROC, 18.5 to 25.3% in micro-AUPRC and 10.6 to 24.1% in MCC. Its ranking is also up to 85% more stable across folding tools.

AI.tldr: EMBER predicts TCR–pMHC binding from independently folded monomer structures as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, avoiding docked complexes and the placement error they introduce.
AI.motivation: Structure-based TCR–pMHC binding predictors rely on co-folded docked complexes and read binding from the contact surface, so any structural deviation from the folding tool propagates into every downstream feature (placement error dominating predictions).
AI.method: EMBER folds TCR and pMHC independently, encodes each as a SE(3)-invariant residue graph, and compares their learned representations without a shared coordinate frame; relative pose is never an input. Preprocessing costs O(N+M) monomer folds versus O(NM) for complex-based predictors.
AI.result: Under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER ranks first on every metric under all four folding tools: +0.9–14.4% micro-AUROC, +18.5–25.3% micro-AUPRC, +10.6–24.1% MCC; ranking up to 85% more stable across folding tools.
AI.conclusion: Removing the docked complex as an input eliminates placement-error propagation while improving accuracy, robustness to folding tool choice, and computational efficiency.

title: Turning-Point Impact Compromises the Biomechanical Integrity of Cortical Bone during Oscillating Sawing
comment: 35 pages, 8 figures. Pre-peer-review version of an article published in Annals of Biomedical Engineering
summary: Purpose Oscillating bone sawing is widely used in orthopedic procedures such as total knee arthroplasty, where preservation of the mechanical integrity of the prepared bone surface is essential for implant stability. However, the reciprocating motion of oscillating saws can generate transient impact events near trajectory turning points, potentially inducing surface damage and reducing local load-bearing capacity. This study aimed to investigate the biomechanical consequences of turning-point impact loading during oscillating bone sawing. Methods Oscillating sawing experiments were performed on bovine cortical bone using a conventional trajectory and an optimized trajectory designed to suppress turning-point impacts. Dynamic sawing forces were measured to quantify impact events. Surface damage on the groove wall surface was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and optical imaging. Local and global mechanical responses were evaluated using compression tests. Results The conventional trajectory produced pronounced periodic force spikes and generated extensive surface cracks and breakout regions. These impact-dominated events were associated with reduced local compressive strength of the prepared bone surface. In contrast, the optimized trajectory significantly suppressed peak impact forces, resulting in smoother groove wall surfaces with fewer defects. Consequently, the optimized trajectory increased the local compressive strength (p < 0.001) and improved the global compressive strength of the specimens (p = 0.001), while the elastic modulus remained largely unchanged. Conclusion Turning-point impacts during oscillating bone sawing compromise the biomechanical integrity of cortical bone by promoting surface damage and reducing local load-bearing capacity. Suppressing these transient impacts helps preserve the mechanical integrity of surgically prepared bone surfaces.

AI.tldr: Turning-point impacts in oscillating bone sawing cause surface cracks and reduce local compressive strength of cortical bone; an optimized saw trajectory suppresses these impacts and preserves biomechanical integrity.
AI.motivation: Oscillating saws are standard in total knee arthroplasty, where bone surface integrity governs implant stability. The reciprocating motion produces transient impact events near trajectory turning points that may damage the prepared surface, but the biomechanical consequences had not been characterized.
AI.method: Oscillating sawing experiments on bovine cortical bone comparing a conventional trajectory versus an optimized trajectory designed to suppress turning-point impacts. Dynamic sawing forces quantified impact events; SEM and optical imaging characterized groove wall surface damage; compression tests assessed local and global mechanical responses.
AI.result: Conventional trajectory caused periodic force spikes, extensive surface cracks, and breakout regions with reduced local compressive strength. The optimized trajectory significantly lowered peak impact forces, produced smoother groove walls with fewer defects, increased local compressive strength (p < 0.001) and global compressive strength (p = 0.001), while elastic modulus was largely unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Turning-point impacts compromise cortical bone integrity by inducing surface damage and lowering load-bearing capacity; suppressing these transient impacts preserves the mechanical integrity of surgically prepared bone surfaces.

title: What I Disbelieve: Quantifying Belief With Negative Ranking Functions
summary: A challenge in exploring the psychology of human uncertainty is its measurement and quantification. Prior work has focused almost exclusively on probability, while the formal theories developed in philosophy are rarely tested. We tested Wolfgang Spohn's ranking theory, a normative account in which belief is graded by ordinal ranks of disbelief that combine by minimization rather than addition, as a descriptive model of human belief. Across six experiments, participants assigned ranks of disbelief to propositions involving personal experience, chance devices, sequential learning, and an Ellsberg urn. Ranks were reliable and, through the theory's two-sided rank function, distinguished belief, disbelief, and suspension of judgment. Participants respected the Law of Negation, never disbelieving both a proposition and its complement, in every task except a lottery. Disjunctions did not follow the theory's Law of Disjunction. Instead of taking the minimum rank of the disjuncts, participants averaged them. In a learning task, ranks aligned more closely than did subjective probabilities with objective probabilities. In an Ellsberg Urn scenario, the paradoxical behavior seen with betting was markedly reduced by ranks. We conclude that human belief has the bipolar, negation-respecting structure that ranking theory proposes, but combines disjuncts by averaging rather than by minimization. As a clear account of human belief dynamics with metrics that can be reliably measured, Ranking Theory provides a valuable framework for investigating and contrasting probabilistic and non-probabilistic accounts of human belief.

AI.tldr: Six experiments test Spohn's ranking theory as a descriptive model of human belief; ranks are reliable and bipolar with the proposed negations and averaging for disjunctions rather than Spohn's minimization.
AI.motivation: The psychology of human uncertainty has been measured almost exclusively via probability, and formal philosophical theories of belief are rarely tested empirically. The authors ask whether Spohn's ranking theory can serve as a descriptive, measurable account of human belief.
AI.method: Across six experiments, participants assigned ordinal ranks of disbelief to propositions involving personal experience, chance devices, sequential learning, and an Ellsberg urn. The authors examined the two-sided rank function's ability to distinguish belief, disbelief, and suspension of judgment, and compared ranks against subjective probabilities in learning and Ellsberg tasks.
AI.result: Ranks were reliable and distinguished belief, disbelief, and suspension of judgment. Participants respected the Law of Negation except in a lottery task. Disjunctions violated the Law of Disjunction: instead of the minimum rank of disjuncts, participants averaged them. In learning, ranks tracked objective probabilities better than subjective probabilities did. In the Ellsberg urn scenario, the betting paradox was markedly reduced when ranks were used.
AI.conclusion: Human belief has the bipolar, negation-respecting structure that ranking theory proposes, but disjuncts are combined by averaging rather than by minimization. With metrics that can be reliably measured, Ranking Theory offers a valuable framework for investigating and contrasting probabilistic and non-probabilistic accounts of human belief.

title: An Open Reliability Atlas of Sensitivity and Failure Modes in the Pulse Physiology Engine
comment: 81 pages, 10 figures, 21 tables; main text followed by the Supplementary Information. Code: https://github.com/sadc-lab/pulse_reliability_atlas
summary: Pulse is an actively maintained open-source adult-physiology simulator, yet its maintainers report no formal sensitivity analysis of its operational inputs. We present the first open reliability atlas across its critical-care envelope: Morris elementary-effects sampling of seven inputs, four severity scenarios, male and female bodies (1,280 simulations). Sensitivity is skewed: three inputs carry a median 93% of each output's total. A four-flag classifier reveals failure modes: two operator-actionable, one sex-stratified. Tidal-volume oscillation (20.6% of runs) is consistent with patient-ventilator dyssynchrony; locking the VC-AC trigger to -2 cmH2O collapses that variability. At FiO2 = 1.0, transient hyperoxia makes 120-second runs underestimate plateau PaO2; 300-second healthy-lung reruns give a median 643 mmHg. Solver divergence was all-male in an input-extreme regime (20/1,280); reducing the male blood-volume baseline to the 4,082 mL floor eliminated it. Runs and flags are released openly, showing users which regions need checking before training on Pulse output.

AI.tldr: First open sensitivity/reliability atlas of the Pulse adult-physiology simulator, using Morris elementary-effects sampling (7 inputs, 4 severity scenarios, 2 sexes, 1,280 runs) to identify which inputs dominate outputs, which failure modes occur, and how to mitigate them.
AI.motivation: Pulse is an actively maintained open-source adult-physiology simulator, but its maintainers report no formal sensitivity analysis of its operational inputs. Users therefore lack guidance on which input regions produce unreliable outputs before training on Pulse data.
AI.method: Morris elementary-effects screening of seven operational inputs across the critical-care envelope, crossed with four severity scenarios and male/female bodies (1,280 simulations). A four-flag classifier was applied to categorize failure modes, and targeted mitigation experiments (trigger setting, run duration, blood-volume baseline) were run.
AI.result: Sensitivity is highly skewed: three inputs carry a median 93% of each output's total sensitivity. Four failure flags emerged: two operator-actionable and one sex-stratified. Tidal-volume oscillation affected 20.6% of runs (consistent with patient-ventilator dyssynchrony) and disappeared when the VC-AC trigger was locked to -2 cmH2O. At FiO2 = 1.0, 120-s runs underestimated plateau PaO2 due to transient hyperoxia; 300-s healthy-lung reruns gave a median of 643 mmHg. Solver divergence occurred only in males in an input-extreme regime (20/1,280) and was eliminated by lowering the male blood-volume baseline to the 4,082 mL floor.
AI.conclusion: Pulse sensitivity is dominated by a few inputs, and several reliability failure modes are diagnosable and fixable via specific configuration changes. All runs and flags are released openly so users can identify which regions require checking before training on Pulse output.

title: Spatially Informed and Direction Sensitive Representation Learning for Spatial Transcriptomics
comment: This manuscript has been accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap (AI4DD)
summary: Cellular states are shaped by both intrinsic gene expression programs and the spatial microenvironment in which cells reside. Spatial transcriptomics makes this context measurable, but effective representation learning requires capturing both spatially informative molecular signals and intercellular organization. Existing approaches address these challenges only partially: conventional gene selection can overlook spatially structured signals, while methods for encoding cell-cell relationships often either reduce a cell's microenvironment to proximity alone, discarding direction, or rely on absolute coordinates tied to an arbitrary tissue frame. Consequently, cells with similar neighbor distances but distinct spatial organization may receive overly similar representations, despite experiencing different biological contexts that shape their cellular states. We introduce Tessera, a spatial representation learning framework that addresses both molecular selection and cellular context. Tessera combines spatially informed gene selection with a geometric inductive bias that contextualizes each cell within its local tissue environment. By modeling relative cell-cell relationships, Tessera is translation-invariant while preserving direction, allowing neighboring cells to contribute differently according to their spatial context and cellular state. Across held-out tissues and technologies, Tessera outperforms existing spatial foundation models in representation quality and generalizes zero-shot to contexts up to $16\times$ larger than those seen during training.

AI.tldr: Tessera is a spatial representation learning framework for spatial transcriptomics that combines spatially informed gene selection with a direction-preserving, translation-invariant geometric inductive bias for relative cell-cell relationships, outperforming existing spatial foundation models and generalizing zero-shot to much larger tissue contexts.
AI.motivation: Cellular states depend on intrinsic gene expression and the spatial microenvironment. Spatial transcriptomics makes this measurable, but existing methods only partially capture it: conventional gene selection can miss spatially structured signals, and cell-cell relationship encoders either reduce microenvironments to proximity alone (discarding direction) or rely on absolute coordinates tied to an arbitrary tissue frame. As a result, cells with similar neighbor distances but different spatial organization get overly similar representations despite distinct biological contexts.
AI.method: Tessera combines (1) spatially informed gene selection that captures spatially structured molecular signals, and (2) a geometric inductive bias that contextualizes each cell within its local tissue environment by modeling relative cell-cell relationships. This makes the model translation-invariant while preserving direction, so neighbors contribute differently according to their spatial context and cellular state.
AI.result: Across held-out tissues and technologies, Tessera outperforms existing spatial foundation models in representation quality and generalizes zero-shot to contexts up to 16x larger than those seen during training.
AI.conclusion: Tessera addresses both molecular selection and cellular context, providing more effective spatial representations that generalize across tissues and scales, and highlighting the value of direction-aware, frame-invariant geometric modeling in spatial transcriptomics.

title: Anchored Exploration in Product Evolution: A Phylogenetic Network Framework for Semiconductor Designs
summary: We develop a product phylogenetic network framework for examining anchored exploration. Using 102,465 semiconductor products grouped into 45,996 design families, we distinguish accumulated design continuity (Anchor) from externally precedented feature additions (horizontal transfer, HT). Fitted regressions yield non-monotonic relationships for HT occurrence and descendant carriage, alongside increasing within-family carriage over observed support. These patterns connect technological trajectories and recombination by distinguishing the continuity associated with incorporating external features from that associated with reproducing them in subsequent products.

AI.tldr: This paper builds a "product phylogenetic network" framework to study anchored exploration in technology, decomposing semiconductor product evolution into accumulated design continuity ("Anchor") versus externally sourced feature additions ("horizontal transfer," HT). Using 102,465 products in 45,996 design families, regressions reveal non-monotonic HT patterns and rising within-family carriage with support, linking technological trajectories to recombination.
AI.motivation: Existing work on technological trajectories and recombination lacks a way to separate continuity inherited within a lineage from features obtained externally. The authors want a framework that distinguishes the continuity involved in incorporating external features from the continuity involved in reproducing them downstream.
AI.method: A product phylogenetic network framework applied to 102,465 semiconductor products grouped into 45,996 design families, distinguishing accumulated design continuity (Anchor) from externally precedented feature additions (horizontal transfer, HT). Fitted regressions are used to examine HT occurrence and descendant carriage.
AI.result: Regressions yield non-monotonic relationships for both HT occurrence and descendant carriage, alongside increasing within-family carriage over observed support.
AI.conclusion: The framework connects technological trajectories and recombination by separating the continuity associated with incorporating external features from that associated with reproducing them in subsequent products.

title: Ontic state recovery through prediction
summary: We encounter a system through its responses, yet its state concerns how the system is. Predicting further responses promises knowledge beyond what is immediately observed. What that knowledge tells us about the system's state depends on what we mean by a state in the first place. We give this notion a model-relative meaning: a state is the complete response profile over a specified query universe, and configurations agreeing on every query are regarded as the same state. From this perspective, a learned state is understood through the distinctions between these profiles that it retains. Prediction concerns selected observations; recovery concerns the profile as a whole. We examine their relationship through query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and the choice of prediction targets. Synthetic systems with known response laws and neural recordings provide complementary settings for this investigation. The aim is to clarify how prediction can become a way of knowing a system, and what it would mean for a learned state to preserve the state being studied.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-relative notion of "state" as the complete response profile over a specified query universe, then examines the relationship between prediction (selected observations) and recovery (the whole profile) via query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and prediction-target choice, using synthetic systems and neural recordings.
AI.motivation: Systems are known only through responses, yet their "state" concerns how they are. The knowledge gained by predicting further responses depends on what a state means, so this foundational notion needs clarification—especially how prediction relates to knowing a system and what it means for a learned state to preserve the studied state.
AI.method: Defines state model-relatively: as the full response profile over a specified query universe, with configurations agreeing on all queries considered the same state. A learned state is characterized by which distinctions between profiles it retains. The analysis uses three lenses—query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and prediction-target choice—applied to synthetic systems with known response laws and to neural recordings.
AI.result: The conceptual framework reframes prediction as prediction of selected observations and recovery as identification of the whole profile, and shows how their relationship depends on query choice and state-space structure across complementary synthetic and neural settings.
AI.conclusion: The work aims to clarify how prediction can be a way of knowing a system and what it means for a learned state to preserve the state under study, grounding state and recovery in the observer's query universe.

title: Representing short-term movement to reveal animal identity and learning progress
comment: The first three authors contribute equally to this work
summary: How learning progresses over time and varies across individuals is a longstanding question in cognitive and behavioral science. However, a major challenge is identifying observable behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression. Existing approaches commonly rely on predefined behavioral features or task-level performance, while fine-scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals remain less explored. In this paper, we ask: can short-term movement trajectories reveal learning progress and individual identity? We introduce a self-supervised representation learning framework built on a simple hypothesis: behavioral characteristics associated with identity and learning remain relatively stable over nearby time intervals. Using temporal proximity as supervision, our framework learns compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defining behavioral states or kinematic features. Using behavior data from freely behaving rats, we show that the learned representations not only improve prediction of identity and learning-related readouts over existing methods, but also provide a tool for investigating broader scientific questions about when and how these signals appear in behavior. Specifically, trajectories as short as one second contain informative learning and identity signals. Egocentric pose dynamics are more predictive of identity, whereas allocentric motion is more predictive of learning-related variation, and both signals are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort. We further use a representation-conditioned diffusion model to inspect movement patterns associated with identity and learning progress. Our findings establish short-term movement as an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Our code is available at https://github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.

AI.tldr: Short-term (even ~1s) movement trajectories, encoded via self-supervised temporal-proximity representation learning, reveal both individual identity and learning progress in freely behaving rats.
AI.motivation: Identifying behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression over time and across individuals is a longstanding challenge. Existing methods rely on predefined features or task-level performance, neglecting fine-scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals.
AI.method: A self-supervised representation learning framework (TRAIL) using temporal proximity as supervision, learning compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defined behavioral states or kinematic features. Applied to freely behaving rats; a representation-conditioned diffusion model inspects associated movement patterns.
AI.result: Learned representations improve prediction of identity and learning-related readouts over existing methods. Trajectories as short as one second carry informative signals; egocentric pose dynamics better predict identity, allocentric motion better predicts learning variation, and both are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort.
AI.conclusion: Short-term movement is an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Code available at github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.

title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
summary: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

AI.tldr: Magnolia is a persistent-memory LLM agent framework for computational chemistry that uses a three-tier memory system (session → project → cross-project rules) to guide docking, MD, and quantum chemistry workflows, outperforming memory-less runs on controlled replay checks.
AI.motivation: Chemistry has entered a high-data regime with growing automation and digital, precision workflows. Chemists face an ever-increasing volume of data and findings (including negative results), so dedicated scientific agents are needed to guide them—yet existing agents lack persistent, validated memory to carry learnings across runs and projects.
AI.method: Magnolia is a persistent-memory AI agent framework integrating computational protocols (docking to quantum chemistry), lab notebooks, and chat logs via LLMs. Its three-tier memory: session-level observations are auto-captured and distilled into structured learnings; confirmed learnings are elevated to project-tier entries; human-validated entries are promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and give direct chemical feedback. Evaluated on four case studies plus controlled replays.
AI.result: Across four case studies—quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), MD of butane and modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign—Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, with four promoted cross-project rules. In controlled replays of four tasks, memory-enabled runs passed checks that memory-less runs failed (e.g., 10/10 docking-configuration checks vs. 1–4/10).
AI.conclusion: By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, Magnolia streamlines docking, MD, and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, accelerating access to computational (bio)chemistry.

title: BARRR: Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression for Multi-View Multi-Cohort Data
summary: Bidimensional data integration across multiple cohorts (i.e., sample groups) and views (i.e., sources or modalities) is crucial in biomedical research to derive holistic insights from heterogeneous datasets. However, most existing integrative methods focus on a single dimension, such as multi-view integration across distinct sources or multi-cohort integration across distinct sample groups. Existing approaches for bidimensional integration are scarce and predominantly unsupervised, overlooking the valuable insights offered by covariates. To address this gap, we introduce the Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression (baRRR) method. Our approach models covariate-related and unrelated effects concurrently, while also decomposing effect levels (global, partially shared, and individual) across both dimensions. Extensive simulations demonstrate the advantages of our method with respect to signal recovery, outcome prediction, and missing data imputation. We apply our approach to data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), using somatic mutations as covariates to inform patterns of variability across different omics platforms and cancer types. These studies highlight its potential as a robust and adaptable tool for integrative analysis in biomedical research.

AI.tldr: baRRR (Bidimensional Augmented Reduced Rank Regression) enables supervised bidimensional integration across cohorts and views, jointly modeling covariate-related and unrelated effects decomposed into global, partially shared, and individual levels.
AI.motivation: Most integrative methods handle only one dimension (multi-view OR multi-cohort), and rare bidimensional approaches are unsupervised, ignoring covariates that carry valuable signal. A supervised, bidimensional method is needed.
AI.method: A reduced-rank regression framework augmented to model covariate-related and unrelated effects simultaneously, while decomposing effect levels (global, partially shared, individual) along both the cohort and view dimensions.
AI.result: Extensive simulations show advantages in signal recovery, outcome prediction, and missing data imputation. Applied to TCGA data using somatic mutations as covariates to inform variability across omics platforms and cancer types.
AI.conclusion: baRRR is a robust, adaptable tool for supervised bidimensional integrative analysis in biomedical research.

title: An exact coexistence criterion for stochastic Lotka--Volterra systems with Volterra--Lyapunov stable interactions
summary: We consider stochastic Lotka-Volterra systems $dX=\mathrm{Diag}(X)(α+AX)dt+\mathrm{Diag}(X)ΓdB$ with nondegenerate noise and a Volterra-Lyapunov stable interaction matrix $A$, that is, $DA+A^\top D\prec 0$ for some positive diagonal matrix $D$. This class covers every self-limited predator-prey food web that is conservative in the sense of Volterra, in particular every such web whose interaction graph is a forest. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for invariant coexistence: the process has an invariant probability measure on $(0,\infty)^n$, that is, a stationary distribution under which all species have positive densities, if and only if $m=-A^{-1}β$ is positive, where $β=α-\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{diag}(ΓΓ^\top)$ is the vector of noise-corrected growth rates. This measure is then unique and ergodic, has mean $m$, and attracts every interior initial condition exponentially fast in total variation. Thus environmental noise affects coexistence only through the Itô shift $α\mapstoβ$, and the criterion is the exact counterpart of the feasibility criterion for the deterministic system $\dot x=\mathrm{Diag}(x)(β+Ax)$. Both directions rest on the fact that, for Lotka-Volterra systems, invasion rates are affine in the mean of the underlying measure. Necessity follows from an exact formula for the means of invariant measures supported on faces of the orthant. Sufficiency follows from the persistence theorem of Hening and Nguyen, for which the explicit weights $Dm$ give a stochastic counterpart of Hofbauer's average Lyapunov function, so that no enumeration of the invariant measures on the boundary is required. Applied to subcommunities, the result also characterizes every stationary regime in which some species are absent.

AI.tldr: For stochastic Lotka-Volterra systems with nondegenerate noise and a Volterra-Lyapunov stable interaction matrix, an invariant coexistence measure exists (uniquely, ergodic, mean m) if and only if m = -A^{-1}β is positive, matching the deterministic feasibility criterion with noise only shifting α to β.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to characterize coexistence in stochastic Lotka-Volterra systems under environmental noise, and to determine how noise alters the deterministic feasibility condition for persistent coexistence.
AI.method: The analysis uses the affine-in-mean property of invasion rates for Lotka-Volterra systems. Necessity uses an exact formula for means of invariant measures on faces of the orthant. Sufficiency applies the persistence theorem of Hening and Nguyen, using explicit weights Dm as a stochastic analog of Hofbauer's average Lyapunov function, avoiding boundary enumeration.
AI.result: An invariant probability measure on the positive orthant exists if and only if m = -A^{-1}β > 0, where β is the noise-corrected growth rate. This measure is unique, ergodic, has mean m, and attracts every interior initial condition exponentially fast in total variation. The result extends via subcommunities to characterize all stationary regimes with absent species.
AI.conclusion: Environmental noise affects coexistence only through the Itô shift α → β, yielding an exact stochastic counterpart of the deterministic feasibility criterion for Diag(x)(β+Ax). The framework also characterizes stationary regimes with partially absent species.

title: VGL-stGen: Learning a shared multimodal model for lung histology and spatial transcriptomics
summary: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model adapted from a pretrained medical vision-language model using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training integrates image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, and gene-conditioned pseudo-labels transfer transcriptomic cell-type supervision to histology images. One deployed checkpoint supports thirteen evaluated tasks spanning tissue and cell-type classification, gene prediction and conditional expression completion from combinations of histology, cell identity and observed gene expression. Task-specific decoding produces categorical labels, gene lists and structured expression levels. For conditional completion, fixing queried gene identities and predicting their levels autoregressively improves structured prediction. Controlled adaptation shows that restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens can further improve image-conditioned completion. Image-permutation experiments indicate that correctly paired histology adds information beyond observed expression. External classification relies partly on computational references with shared annotation lineage, and some H&E sources were exposed during cancer training or model development. Within these conditions, VGL-stGen demonstrates how a medical vision-language backbone can learn from spatial transcriptomics and histology to connect tissue morphology and molecular states through shared generative modeling.

AI.tldr: VGL-stGen is a multimodal large language model built from a pretrained medical vision-language model and adapted on paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics, enabling unified tissue/cell-type classification, gene prediction, and conditional expression completion.
AI.motivation: Linking tissue morphology with molecular states is challenging; the authors aim to show that a medical vision-language backbone can learn such connections from spatial transcriptomics paired with histology.
AI.method: Adapts a pretrained medical VLM using paired lung H&E and spatial transcriptomics with single-cell references. Training uses image-expression and expression-cell-type pairs, plus gene-conditioned pseudo-labels to transfer cell-type supervision to images. A single checkpoint handles 13 tasks via task-specific decoding (categorical labels, gene lists, structured expression).
AI.result: Autoregressive completion with fixed queried gene identities improves structured prediction; restricting supervision to requested expression-level tokens improves image-conditioned completion in controlled adaptation; image-permutation shows paired histology adds information beyond observed expression.
AI.conclusion: Under acknowledged limits (dependence on computational references with shared annotation lineage; some H&E sources seen during training), VGL-stGen demonstrates a generative framework connecting tissue morphology and molecular states.

title: Generic finiteness of solutions to parametrized systems of generalized polynomial inequalities
summary:
We study parametrized systems of $\mathit{generalized}$ polynomial inequalities, $(c \circ x^B) \in C$, for a positive variable vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^n_>$, a $\mathit{real}$ exponent matrix $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$, a positive parameter vector $c \in \mathbb{R}^m_>$, and a positive, blunt coefficient cone $C \subset \mathbb{R}^m_>$. This setting includes (i) generalized polynomial equations, $A \, (c \circ x^B) = 0$, arising e.g. from power-law dynamical systems with real exponents (and involving a real coefficient matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n' \times m}$), and (ii) generalized semi-algebraic sets.
  Our main result guarantees the generic finiteness of solutions modulo unavoidable exponential fibers. Building on a framework for parametrized $\mathit{polynomial}$ systems developed by Müller and Regensburger, we reformulate the problem as a system of $\mathit{binomial}$ equations on the coefficient set $P = C \cap Δ\subseteq \mathbb{R}^m_>$, where $Δ$ is a product of (standard) simplices. Solvability is governed by the monomial-dependency subspace $D$.
  Using elementary arguments from analysis and topology, including a logarithmic boundary analysis and Sard's theorem, we control the accumulation of solutions on the boundary and in the interior of $P$. We show that, if $\dim P \le \dim D$, then generically in both the measure-theoretic and topological sense, there are finitely many solutions on $P$ (and hence finitely many exponential fibers of solutions in $\mathbb{R}^n_>$).
  As an application, we prove generic finiteness of steady states (within forward-invariant sets) for parametrized power-law dynamical systems with real exponents.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that parametrized systems of generalized polynomial inequalities (and equations) over positive variables generically have finitely many solutions modulo unavoidable exponential fibers, provided the dimension of the coefficient set P does not exceed the dimension of the monomial-dependency subspace D.
AI.motivation: Parametrized generalized polynomial (power-law) systems with real exponents arise in dynamical systems and generalized semi-algebraic sets, but their solution structure is poorly understood. The authors aim to establish generic finiteness of solutions modulo exponential fibers, extending Müller–Regensburger's polynomial framework to the real-exponent, inequality setting.
AI.method: They reformulate (c∘x^B) ∈ C as a system of binomial equations on the coefficient set P = C ∩ Δ (Δ a product of simplices), where solvability is governed by the monomial-dependency subspace D. Using analysis/topology arguments—logarithmic boundary analysis and Sard's theorem—they control accumulation of solutions on the boundary and interior of P.
AI.result: If dim P ≤ dim D, then generically (both measure-theoretically and topologically) there are finitely many solutions on P, hence finitely many exponential fibers of solutions in R^n_>. As an application, they prove generic finiteness of steady states within forward-invariant sets for parametrized power-law dynamical systems with real exponents.
AI.conclusion: The dimension condition dim P ≤ dim D guarantees generic finiteness of solutions modulo exponential fibers, generalizing prior polynomial results to real-exponent generalized polynomial inequalities and yielding generic finiteness of steady states in power-law dynamical systems.
